segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Most meetings get booked with a title, a time and nothing else. The few that do have an agenda have nobody enforcing it, because the person who could is the person talking. So we built a chair that will not let you schedule a meeting without an agenda, and then sits in the call and holds you to it. Including me. Watch.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Karen, set up a meeting with Artem tomorrow at ten. Thirty minutes.

segments.speaker: karen
segments.text: There's no agenda in that brief. Karen won't put a meeting in three people's calendars without one. What does this call have to decide? Name the topics below, with who owns each.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: A title, a time, a length, and nothing about what it is for. She refuses. And notice the boxes are still there: she is not blocking me, she is asking the one question the meeting needs. A chair that only says no is just an obstacle.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Karen, set up a meeting with Artem in fifteen minutes, fifteen minutes long, called gavel live demo. Three topics. One: solution and architecture, five minutes, I present it. Two: open discussion, six minutes, I want both Artem and me heard on it. Three: roadmap, four minutes, I present it.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Every topic comes back with an owner, a time budget, and a type. Rows one and three are presentations. Row two is a discussion, and it names who has to be heard on it: Artem, and me. The parse is a draft. The table is the contract.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: How hard she chairs is a dial. Low, medium, high. On medium she waits for a pause. On high she cuts in mid-sentence, and after a warning she is allowed to mute. And nobody is exempt. Not the organizer, not me. If the host is the one running over, the host is the one who gets chaired. I am leaving it on high.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Real invite, real calendar file, real mailbox. And the invite is not what I dictated. I dictated a paragraph. They get this: purpose in one line, every topic numbered, with an owner, a time budget, and who must be heard on it. The agenda has teeth before anybody joins.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Accepted, and it is in my calendar. And the invite carries two links, not one. One drops me straight into the Discord call. The other opens the meeting room.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: This is the room, and it is the page you put on the shared screen. Karen on the left, the agenda under her, topic one already struck through. On the right, the topic that is actually running: how much of its six minutes it has had, and who is holding the floor right now. Underneath, what the room decided, what is still open, and what she parked.

segments.speaker: karen
segments.text: Good afternoon. This is gavel live demo, fifteen minutes, three topics. First: solution and architecture, five minutes, presented by Vitaly. Vitaly, the floor is yours.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Nobody typed start. She opened the meeting herself.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Three moves. Hear: she is in the Discord call as a participant, audio goes to SLNG for speech to text, turns land in Postgres and Redis. Think: this is the part people assume is a model, and isn't. Whether to interrupt is plain code. Who has held the floor, for how long, against the agenda's own budget. Deterministic, testable, and it runs every two hundred and fifty milliseconds. Mastra and Nebius are only asked for the words. The decision was already made. Then text to speech back into the same call, and fal lip-syncs her face. Six containers behind Traefik. One of them knows what Discord is. That is the whole reason this moves to Teams.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: And honestly the interesting part is the cost curve, because once you are running six containers you start asking whether it is cheaper on a reserved instance or spot, and I priced this out against three providers last month, and the pricing pages are all deliberately incomparable, which is a whole separate rant, actually let me tell you about the egress fees...

segments.speaker: karen
segments.text: Vitaly, parked for later: cloud pricing. Back to solution and architecture: what does the room need to understand first?

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: That was eight seconds. I did not cue her. And notice she parked it rather than binned it. She wrote that line just now, it is not a canned string.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Artem, you have been building the Discord side. What breaks first at scale?

segments.speaker: artem
segments.text: The voice connection, before anything else. Discord gives you one gateway per guild and the audio arrives as per-speaker Opus packets, so the first thing that breaks is not the model, it is decoding four people at once and keeping their streams apart. We buffer per speaker and hand SLNG a clean mono stream each, and that is fine for six people in a room. At thirty it is not, because speech to text cost is linear in speakers, so we would push voice activity detection to the edge and only transcribe whoever holds the floor. The second one is the tick. The brain evaluates every two hundred and fifty milliseconds against the agenda, and that loop is cheap, but it reads the last two minutes of turns out of Redis every time. At a hundred concurrent meetings we would keep that window in memory per session and only write through. And the third is the one nobody expects: reconnects. Discord drops a voice websocket every so often, and if you rejoin without carrying the floor state over, the chair forgets who has been talking and stops interrupting exactly when it matters.

segments.speaker: karen
segments.text: Thank you Artem. Vitaly, you have not spoken on this topic yet, and the agenda says you must be heard. Your turn.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Sixty seconds, one voice, and the chair moved the floor. Nobody in this room had to be the person who interrupts.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: Discord is a demo choice, not a product choice. One container knows what a voice call is. Everything else is platform agnostic by construction. Teams is where this actually belongs: an add-on inside the suite where the calendar, the agenda and the org chart already live. And the category is not meeting notes. Notes are a record of what happened. This changes what happens, inside the hour, while it can still be fixed. Time governance, sitting on top of a calendar that already knows what the meeting was for.

segments.speaker: vitaly
segments.text: So: I asked for a meeting the way everybody asks for a meeting, and it said no. I said what it was for, and three people got an agenda with an owner on every line. It opened the call itself. It caught me going off topic in eight seconds. And it took the floor off the person who had held it for a minute and gave it to the person who had not spoken. It never wrote my agenda. It refused to work without one, and then it held me to it. That is a role every company needs and nobody can afford to staff. Thank you.
